summary:
Región del Libertador Bernardo O'Higgins stands under Chile's national framework. Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019: adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, applicants aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and those under 14 cannot use the law although the statute recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, a ruling that applies only to that case.

The dedicated Chile dossier published by Outright International on 12 March 2026 contains no O'Higgins-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding, so this regional assessment rests on national law and on the O'Higgins row of the national case table.

The protective layer is substantial. The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates have offered a third sex option for intersex children since 2006.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, and the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombud for children, while the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

Transphobic violence remains documented nationally. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

For this region specifically, Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026) records Libertador General Bernardo O'Higgins at 1.57% of nationally documented abuse cases, a year-on-year rise of 9.09% in 2025. Nationally the report counts 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, the highest in 24 years at +27.1%; only Valparaíso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) fell while the other 14 regions rose. Movilh reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate.
tangentialFactors:
O'Higgins holds a small share of the national total, 1.57% of documented abuse cases in 2025, which places it among the lower-volume regions rather than among the principal sites of reported incidents. The direction of travel matters more than the share: the region's figure rose 9.09% year on year while the national count climbed 27.1% to 3,620 cases, the highest in 24 years.

The national pattern is one of dispersion. Only two of Chile's 16 regions recorded a decline in 2025, Valparaíso at -17.56% and Metropolitana at -14.35%, while the remaining 14 rose. Movilh interprets this as hatred moving into regions with less public debate, which is the basis for treating O'Higgins as a mid-share jurisdiction with an upward trajectory rather than a low-risk one.

Comparative context for a visitor: Chile's statutory position is stronger than that of most neighbouring jurisdictions in the region, with self-determination-based legal gender recognition, marriage equality, and explicit hate-crime aggravation, yet the enforcement picture is uneven and the political environment is contested. Budget votes and non-binding legislative reports in 2025 show that protective programmes can be defunded without any change to the underlying statutes.

The 2024 share for O'Higgins is not reproduced in the 2025 edition of the Movilh report, so a two-year regional trend line cannot be drawn from this source alone.

Residents of O'Higgins use the same national channels as the rest of Chile: name and sex changes are filed directly with the Civil Registry for adults, and family courts handle applications for those aged 14 to 18. The Constitutional Court's 9 April 2025 ruling on the 'over 14 years old' wording applies only to the case before it, so the statutory pathway for younger children remains unsettled in practice.

Healthcare access for resident trans people runs through the public system, which has funded reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013 and requires care centres to register patients by social name under the 2011 Ministry of Health circular. The Ministry of Health-run support programme continues after Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program in November 2025, and Crece con Orgullo has served children and adolescents aged 3 to 17 since 2023. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring new hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines appear, though the Medical College has stated that physicians may still prescribe.

Detained residents are covered by the Gendarmería de Chile protocol on gender identity, which provides placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations under a standing oversight committee.

Discrimination complaints in the region are captured in Movilh's national reporting, where O'Higgins accounted for 1.57% of documented cases in 2025. The Zamudio Law supplies the statutory basis for complaints based on sexual orientation, gender identity and, since 2018, gender expression.
